lead: A variational autoencoder (VAE) is a generative model: it learns a distribution over data so you can draw new samples. It keeps the encoder–decoder shape of an autoencoder but replaces the single code with a distribution. The encoder q_φ(z|x) outputs a Gaussian over a latent vector z, a short list of hidden numbers; the decoder p_θ(x|z) turns a code back into data. Training maximizes a lower bound on log p(x) called the ELBO. Uses include image sampling, interpolation, molecule design and speech or text front ends.
prereq: You need: 6.1 autoencoders for the encoder–decoder shape, 6.2 latent variables and likelihood for p(x) = ∫ p(x|z) p(z) dz, and Unit 2 on backpropagation and gradient descent.

sections.h3: Why the code must become a distribution

blocks.text: A plain autoencoder (6.1) maps input x to one code vector and back to x̂. Nothing forces codes of unseen inputs anywhere useful, so decoding a random code gives noise. Generation needs a distribution over codes, not a lookup table.

The VAE fix has two parts. The encoder outputs q_φ(z|x) instead of a point: given x, it says where z is likely. φ is the encoder weights. A fixed prior p(z) = N(0, I) says codes should sit near the origin with unit variance per direction. z has D numbers (D is latent dimension) and I is the identity matrix, so the D dimensions are independent standard normals.

The decoder p_θ(x|z) maps a code to a distribution over inputs; θ is the decoder weights. Together they define p_θ(x) = ∫ p_θ(x|z) p(z) dz. This integral over R^D has no closed form, so maximum likelihood (6.2) cannot be applied directly.
Instead maximize a lower bound. For any q(z|x):
log p_θ(x) ≥ E_{z~q_φ(z|x)}[log p_θ(x|z)] − KL(q_φ(z|x) ‖ p(z))
blocks.where: Left side: log-likelihood of one x. First right term: expected reconstruction log-likelihood, decoding codes sampled from the encoder and scoring x. Second: KL divergence from encoder distribution to prior, in nats; it measures drift from N(0, I). The right side is the ELBO (evidence lower bound). The gap to the left is KL(q_φ(z|x) ‖ p_θ(z|x)), which shrinks as the encoder better approximates the true posterior.

sections.h3: The Gaussian encoder and the closed-form KL

blocks.text: Make q_φ(z|x) a diagonal Gaussian. The encoder ends in two heads of size D: mean vector μ and log-variance vector. Log form keeps output unconstrained and stops variance from going negative; recover σ² = exp(log σ²). Then q_φ(z|x) = N(μ, diag(σ²)).

One sampled z gives an unbiased estimate of E_q[log p_θ(x|z)]. With a Gaussian decoder centred at x̂ with fixed variance c, the term is −‖x − x̂‖²/(2c) plus a constant, so training uses mean squared error. With a Bernoulli decoder over pixels it becomes binary cross-entropy, the same loss as a binary classifier.
For a diagonal Gaussian against N(0, I), the KL has a closed form:
KL(q_φ(z|x) ‖ p(z)) = ½ Σ_{j=1}^{D} (σ_j² + μ_j² − 1 − ln σ_j²)
blocks.where: μ_j and σ_j² are mean and variance of latent dimension j, for j = 1 to D; ln is natural logarithm, so the answer is in nats. The −1 and −ln σ_j² come from the entropy and normalizing constant of the two Gaussians. σ_j² is variance, not standard deviation.

blocks.text: Training minimizes −ELBO summed over the mini-batch. The terms pull against each other: reconstruction wants codes to carry information, KL wants all codes near the prior. That balance keeps the latent space smooth enough to sample new data.
Backpropagation needs a deterministic path from parameters to loss. Drawing z ~ N(μ, diag(σ²)) is random; no gradient flows through it. The reparameterization trick moves randomness outside:
z = μ + σ ⊙ ε,   ε ~ N(0, I)
blocks.where: σ = √σ² is the standard deviation vector, ⊙ is element-wise multiplication, and ε is noise with no parameters. z is now a smooth function of μ and σ, so ∂z/∂μ = 1 and ∂z/∂σ = ε, and gradients reach the encoder.

items: Forward the mini-batch through the encoder to get μ and log σ², both length D.
Draw ε ~ N(0, I), one noise vector per data point.
Set z = μ + σ ⊙ ε and decode to x̂.
Loss = reconstruction error + KL; backprop through μ and σ; update φ and θ.

blocks.text: β-VAE multiplies the KL term by β. β > 1 presses codes harder toward the prior and often disentangles dimensions (one dimension per factor such as smile or pose) at some cost in sharpness; β < 1 favours reconstruction. Conditional VAE (CVAE) feeds label c into both networks, learning q_φ(z|x, c) and p_θ(x|z, c), so you can ask for a digit of class 7.

Sampling: draw z ~ N(0, I) and decode. Interpolation: encode two inputs and decode along the straight line between their μ vectors; outputs morph smoothly because the prior fills the gap. Latent traversal: move one coordinate z_j by a fixed step, hold the rest, and watch which attribute changes.

figure.caption: The dashed arrow carries the KL term, computed in closed form from μ and σ²; the worked example's μ = 1, σ² = 4 give KL = 1.307 nats. Gradients reach both arrows because z = μ + σ ⊙ ε.

spec.title: VAE training path
spec.aria: Data flows from the input through the encoder to Gaussian parameters, a reparameterized sample, the decoder and a reconstruction; the ELBO adds reconstruction loss to the KL term.

examples.question: A VAE has one latent dimension (D = 1). For an input x the encoder outputs μ = 1 and σ² = 4, and the prior is p(z) = N(0, 1). Compute KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z)) in nats and say whether this code is close to the prior.
steps: With D = 1 the KL sum has one term: KL = ½(σ² + μ² − 1 − ln σ²).
Substitute: μ = 1 so μ² = 1; σ² = 4, so σ = 2. The formula takes variance, so 4 goes in.

A KL of 1.307 nats is well above 0, so the code is not close to the prior: it is too wide (variance 4 against 1) and shifted (mean 1 against 0). Training pushes μ toward 0 and pulls σ² toward 1: here μ = 1 comes down and σ² = 4 comes down toward 1. (If σ² had been below 1, the KL term would push it up.)
examples.answer: KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z)) = 1.307 nats, so the code is far from the prior.
examples.check:
import math
mu = 1.0
var = 4.0
kl = 0.5 * (var + mu**2 - 1 - math.log(var))
print(round(kl, 3))

traps: Variance, not standard deviation. The KL uses σ². Putting σ = 2 in as if variance gives ½(2 + 1 − 1 − ln 2) = 0.65 nats, half the right answer. Encoders output log σ² for this reason: exponentiate once and label the result σ².
KL direction. The ELBO has KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z)), not KL(p(z) ‖ q(z|x)). These differ, and only the first has this simple closed form.
The bound is not the likelihood. Maximizing the ELBO maximizes a lower bound on log p(x); the gap is KL(q(z|x) ‖ p_θ(z|x)) and is zero only if the encoder is exact.

Gradients do not flow into ε. In z = μ + σ ⊙ ε, ε is noise, not a parameter, so no gradient flows into ε; gradients flow only into μ and σ. σ is not redrawn, it is recomputed by the encoder; what is redrawn each step is ε. Treating sampled z as a plain network output breaks training.

Calling it a plain autoencoder. A plain autoencoder has no prior and no KL term, so sampling its latent space is unjustified. The KL term is exactly what makes generation possible, and examiners ask for it.

quiz.q: Write the ELBO for one data point x and name its two terms.
quiz.a: log p_θ(x) ≥ E_{q_φ(z|x)}[log p_θ(x|z)] − KL(q_φ(z|x) ‖ p(z)). First term: expected reconstruction log-likelihood. Second: KL from encoder distribution to prior N(0, I).

quiz.q: What does the encoder network output in a VAE, and why is log variance used?
quiz.a: Two vectors of length D: the mean μ and log σ². The log form keeps the output unconstrained, and σ² = exp(log σ²) is always positive.

quiz.q: Why is the reparameterization trick needed in a VAE?
quiz.a: Sampling z ~ N(μ, σ²) is random, and backpropagation cannot pass a gradient through it. Rewriting z = μ + σ ⊙ ε with ε ~ N(0, I) makes z deterministic given μ, σ and ε, so gradients reach encoder parameters.

quiz.q: One latent dimension, encoder gives μ = 2 and σ² = 1, prior N(0, 1). Compute KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z)) in nats.
quiz.a: KL = ½(σ² + μ² − 1 − ln σ²) = ½(1 + 4 − 1 − ln 1) = ½(4) = 2 nats.

quiz.q: Two latent dimensions, μ = (1, −1) and σ² = (1, 1), prior N(0, I). Compute the KL in nats.
quiz.a: Dimension 1: ½(1 + 1 − 1 − 0) = 0.5. Dimension 2: ½(1 + 1 − 1 − 0) = 0.5. Total = 1 nat.

quiz.q: What happens if β in a β-VAE is set very large?
quiz.a: The KL term dominates. The encoder's q(z|x) collapses toward N(0, I) and the decoder learns to ignore z, giving posterior collapse: reconstructions become blurry or averaged. Reconstruction quality falls (reconstruction error rises). Only moderate β > 1 tends to give more independent, interpretable dimensions; at very large β the code is uninformative and interpretability is lost.

quiz.q: Two VAEs train on the same greyscale digits, one with a Bernoulli decoder and one with a Gaussian decoder of fixed variance. Which reconstruction loss does each use, and why?
quiz.a: Bernoulli: pixels scaled to [0, 1] are treated as probabilities, so loss is binary cross-entropy. Gaussian: the term is −‖x − x̂‖²/(2c) plus a constant, so loss is mean squared error. The choice follows the data range and whether pixels behave like counts or real numbers.

beyond: Not for the exam. VQ-VAE swaps the Gaussian code for a learned codebook and now powers audio and image tokenizers; hierarchical VAEs such as NVAE generate high-resolution images. The same ELBO trains diffusion models, where the encoder is a fixed noising process, so time on KL and reparameterization pays off twice. Conditional VAEs generate molecules with requested properties. Search terms: posterior collapse, disentanglement, VQ-VAE, ELBO in diffusion models.
